hero.title: Different agents. One memory.
hero.lede: ai-memory saves project notes for AI coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex. When you start another session, it supplies saved context and tools to search earlier work, so you spend less time re-explaining your project.
facts: Default memory features need no model API key

cards.title: Keep project context between sessions
cards.text: Session observations become searchable notes in a wiki: a collection of plain-text markdown pages you can inspect and edit.

cards.title: Your habits follow you to the next project
cards.text: In single-user mode, recurring preferences can carry across projects. On a shared server this is off until enabled. Project instructions take precedence.

cards.title: {n} coding agents, one memory
cards.text: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and more share one server. What one learned this morning is there for the next one this afternoon.

cards.title: Install, set up, launch
cards.text: A checksum-verified script and ai-memory setup. The server listens on your machine only, and your memory is markdown in a folder you own.

cards.title: Choose how old session notes are kept
cards.text: Unused session pages can be removed automatically. Optional compaction or merging keeps shorter versions; those rewrites can be restored.

cards.title: {score} hit@5 on LongMemEval-S, caveats included
cards.text: Retrieval is scored with a harness that ships in the repository, capture step included. The number says nothing about answer accuracy.

statement: Notes saved by one coding tool are not always available to another. ai-memory keeps project context in a shared store that your agents can search.

continuity.label: What stays when everything else changes
continuity.title: Change everything. Keep what you know.

agents.title: Switch agents mid-task.
agents.text: Quit Claude Code, open Codex in the same directory. It starts with a handoff: what got done, what failed and what is still open.

machines.title: Switch machines.
machines.text: Memory lives in a small server you run: on your laptop, a homelab box, wherever. The project you left on the desktop is the project you resume on the notebook.

wiki.title: Saves searchable project notes.
wiki.text: Hooks are small commands triggered by the agent’s session events. They record observations that become markdown pages. Browse the wiki, search it, or edit it by hand.

items.title: Stop re-explaining your project
items.text: Two commands to install. You need no account and no API key.

how.title: What happens while you work.
how.lede: Capture saves observations from a session. A handoff summarizes unfinished work for the next one, while the project wiki holds longer-lived notes. The default path needs no cloud language model.
how.figureAlt: Diagram: terminals emit observations that are consolidated into markdown pages, searched through fused ranking, and handed off to the next agent. Underneath it all sits a git-backed wiki of plain markdown files.

steps.title: Capture
steps.text: Hooks record prompts and limited tool observations. Recognized credentials are redacted before storage, but filtering can miss sensitive text.

steps.title: Consolidate
steps.text: When a session ends, its observations become a readable markdown page in the project’s wiki.

steps.title: Recall
steps.text: The next session receives a brief and can search saved pages and observations. Retrieved notes can be incomplete or outdated; check important decisions against their sources.

steps.title: Hand off
steps.text: The next session picks up the baton, and only one session can claim it. It works across agents and across every machine that reaches the server.

compare.title: Coming from another tool?
compare.text: Most memory tools need an LLM, a vector store or a graph database before they remember anything. ai-memory needs one binary and a folder.
compare.cta: Full comparison, including where they win
compare.pick: Pick the tool you use today

quickstart.title: Install, set up, then launch your agent.
quickstart.text: There is no sign-up. The default install listens on your machine only, so nothing else can reach it. You can add it to a project that is already under way: the first session imports the agent history you have on disk.

community.text: New here? The contributing page shows where bug reports, pull requests and new agent integrations go.

aging.title: Choose how old session notes are kept.
aging.text: Unused session pages can be removed automatically. You can enable compaction or merging to retain shorter versions without a cloud model. An optional background pass uses your configured language model to merge old pages; compaction and merge rewrites can be restored.
aging.figureAlt: Diagram: reading a page reinforces its retention score. The retention sweep can evict unused session pages, or optionally compact or merge them. Page content can be recovered if it remains in a retained git checkpoint.

profile.title: Your habits follow you to the next project.
profile.text: Each project keeps its own memory. The profile carries how you usually work, learned from your projects on their own, and hands it to every new one at session start, below the repository’s rules. Start a new repository and the agent already knows your baseline.
profile.figureAlt: Diagram: Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode share one project through the memory chip. Three projects feed the chip, which holds the profile, and one arrow leads from it to a new project.

guide.title: Before you connect a project
guide.purpose: This is a tool for people already using AI to work on code. It stores context outside the coding agent so later sessions can retrieve it.
guide.capture: With capture enabled, prompts and limited tool observations are recorded. An empty project can import recent local agent history on first use. In single-user mode, recurring preferences can carry across projects.
guide.boundary: These defaults describe ai-memory. Your coding agent has its own provider connections and data settings.
